entry.title: Expected Information Gain is a Bet Against Uninformative Data
entry.summary:
Expected Information Gain is a Bet Against Uninformative Data

Published on 2026-10-26.

#bayesian-experimental-design

The expected information gain (EIG, Lindley, 1956), the expected reduction in Shannon (or differential) entropy from the prior to the posterior, is a popular objective in Bayesian experimental design. It has several useful interpretations: it is the mutual information between the data and the latent parameters of interest zzz, and it is the expected reduction in Bayes risk for a decision problem under the logarithmic score (see my earlier post on expected information as expected utility). This post is about yet another interpretation: the EIG is the optimal growth rate of a bettor who bets against the null hypothesis that the data are uninformative about zzz.

I begin by reviewing Kelly’s result on betting with side information and its connection to the more general testing-by-betting paradigm, and then show that the EIG is exactly Kelly’s growth rate when the side information is zzz.

A Brief Review of Kelly Betting

Kelly (1956) considered a gambler with access to side information. Suppose that in each round a pair (Yi,Zi)(Y_{i}, Z_{i})(Yi​,Zi​) is drawn i.i.d. from a joint distribution q(y,z)q(y, z)q(y,z), with YiY_{i}Yi​ taking values in a finite set Y\mathcal{Y}Y. The bookmaker knows only the marginal law q(y)q(y)q(y) of the outcome and offers fair odds accordingly: a unit stake on outcome yyy returns 1/q(y)1/q(y)1/q(y) if Yi=yY_{i} = yYi​=y and nothing otherwise. We, however, receive ZiZ_{i}Zi​ over a “private wire” before each round. We start with an initial wealth V0V_{0}V0​, and in each round we observe Zi=zZ_{i} = zZi​=z and stake a fraction b(y∣z)b(y \mid z)b(y∣z) of our current wealth on each y∈Yy \in \mathcal{Y}y∈Y. Kelly asked which strategy bbb maximises the logarithmic rate of growth1 of our wealth, G(b)=lim⁡N→∞1Nlog⁡VNV0,G(b) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{1}{N} \log \frac{V_{N}}{V_{0}},G(b)=N→∞lim​N1​logV0​VN​​, where VNV_{N}VN​ is our wealth after round NNN. Throughout, log⁡\loglog is the natural logarithm; Kelly used base 2, which only changes the units from nats to bits. By the law of large numbers, with probability one we have G(b)=E[log⁡b(Y∣Z)q(Y)]=Eq(z)[KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ q]−KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ b(⋅∣z)]].G(b) = \mathbb{E}\left[\log \frac{b(Y \mid Z)}{q(Y)}\right] = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\Big[\operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, q] - \operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, b(\cdot \mid z)]\Big].G(b)=E[logq(Y)b(Y∣Z)​]=Eq(z)​[KL[q(⋅∣z)∥q]−KL[q(⋅∣z)∥b(⋅∣z)]]. Since the KL divergence is non-negative and zero only when its arguments coincide, Kelly’s result follows immediately: the optimal strategy and the resulting optimal rate of growth are b⋆(y∣z)=q(y∣z),G(b⋆)=Eq(z)[KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ q]]=I(Y;Z).b^{\star}(y \mid z) = q(y \mid z), \qquad G(b^{\star}) = \mathbb{E}_{q(z)}\left[\operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, q]\right] = I(Y; Z).b⋆(y∣z)=q(y∣z),G(b⋆)=Eq(z)​[KL[q(⋅∣z)∥q]]=I(Y;Z). Here I(Y;Z)I(Y; Z)I(Y;Z) is the mutual information between YYY and ZZZ, defined by the middle expression: the average KL divergence of the conditional law of YYY given ZZZ from its marginal law, or equivalently KL⁡[q(y,z) ∥ q(y) q(z)]\operatorname{KL}[q(y, z) \,\Vert\, q(y) \, q(z)]KL[q(y,z)∥q(y)q(z)]. In words, we should bet on each outcome in proportion to our belief in it given what the wire tells us, and our wealth then grows at a rate equal to the mutual information between the wire and the outcome. If the wire carries no information (ZZZ independent of YYY), the best we can do is break even.

Testing by Betting

Kelly’s formulation extends naturally to statistical testing, an idea known as testing by betting (Shafer, 2021; Shafer and Vovk, 2019). To see how, suppose the wire always carries the same message zzz, so that the outcomes are i.i.d. draws from q(⋅∣z)q(\cdot \mid z)q(⋅∣z), while the bookmaker still prices them at qqq. Betting against this bookmaker is then a test of the null hypothesis H0 ⁣:Yi∼qH_{0}\colon Y_{i} \sim qH0​:Yi​∼q against the alternative H1 ⁣:Yi∼q(⋅∣z)H_{1}\colon Y_{i} \sim q(\cdot \mid z)H1​:Yi​∼q(⋅∣z): the bookmaker believes the null, and we measure the evidence against it by how much money we make.

If we follow Kelly’s strategy and bet b⋆(⋅∣z)=q(⋅∣z)b^{\star}(\cdot \mid z) = q(\cdot \mid z)b⋆(⋅∣z)=q(⋅∣z), then in round sss our wealth is multiplied by Es=q(ys∣z)q(ys),E_{s} = \frac{q(y_{s} \mid z)}{q(y_{s})},Es​=q(ys​)q(ys​∣z)​, so starting from V0=1V_{0} = 1V0​=1, our wealth after ttt rounds is Mt=∏s=1tEs=∏s=1tq(ys∣z)q(ys),M_{t} = \prod_{s=1}^{t} E_{s} = \prod_{s=1}^{t} \frac{q(y_{s} \mid z)}{q(y_{s})},Mt​=s=1∏t​Es​=s=1∏t​q(ys​)q(ys​∣z)​, which is simply the likelihood ratio of the data. Since the odds are fair under the null, we cannot expect to make money if the null is true: Eq[Es]=1andEq[Mt+1∣Y1:t]=Mt.\mathbb{E}_{q}[E_{s}] = 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathbb{E}_{q}[M_{t+1} \mid Y_{1:t}] = M_{t}.Eq​[Es​]=1andEq​[Mt+1​∣Y1:t​]=Mt​. That is, MtM_{t}Mt​ is a non-negative martingale under H0H_{0}H0​ with M0=1M_{0} = 1M0​=1, known as a test martingale. By Ville’s inequality, for any α∈(0,1)\alpha \in (0, 1)α∈(0,1), Pq(∃ t ⁣:Mt≥1/α)≤α,\mathbb{P}_{q}\left(\exists\, t \colon M_{t} \geq 1/\alpha\right) \leq \alpha,Pq​(∃t:Mt​≥1/α)≤α, so rejecting H0H_{0}H0​ as soon as our wealth reaches 1/α1/\alpha1/α is a level-α\alphaα test.

Each EsE_{s}Es​ is an e-variable, a non-negative statistic with expectation at most 111 under the null, and MtM_{t}Mt​ is an e-process, a non-negative process satisfying Eq[Mτ]≤1\mathbb{E}_{q}[M_{\tau}] \leq 1Eq​[Mτ​]≤1 for every stopping time τ\tauτ (Ramdas and Wang, 2025). Kelly’s theorem tells us which bet to make when the alternative is true. If Yi∼q(⋅∣z)Y_{i} \sim q(\cdot \mid z)Yi​∼q(⋅∣z), then 1tlog⁡Mt→KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ q]\frac{1}{t} \log M_{t} \to \operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, q]t1​logMt​→KL[q(⋅∣z)∥q] almost surely, so our wealth grows exponentially and we eventually reject the null. Moreover, no other e-variable for this null grows faster. Grünwald et al. (2024) call this the growth-rate optimal (GRO) criterion. For a simple null and a simple alternative, the GRO e-variable is exactly the likelihood ratio q(⋅∣z)/qq(\cdot \mid z)/qq(⋅∣z)/q, and its growth rate is KL⁡[q(⋅∣z) ∥ q]\operatorname{KL}[q(\cdot \mid z) \,\Vert\, q]KL[q(⋅∣z)∥q], the term inside the expectation in Kelly’s growth rate.

The Experimental Design Setting

Let zzz be a latent variable with prior p(z)p(z)p(z). At each step t∈{1,…,T}t \in \{1, \dots, T\}t∈{1,…,T}, the experimenter chooses a design xtx_{t}xt​ according to a policy, xt∼π(⋅∣ht−1)x_{t} \sim \pi(\cdot \mid h_{t-1})xt​∼π(⋅∣ht−1​), and observes an outcome yt∼p(⋅∣z,xt,ht−1)y_{t} \sim p(\cdot \mid z, x_{t}, h_{t-1})yt​∼p(⋅∣z,xt​,ht−1​), where ht=((x1,y1),…,(xt,yt))h_{t} = ((x_{1}, y_{1}), \dots, (x_{t}, y_{t}))ht​=((x1​,y1​),…,(xt​,yt​)) is the history so far and h0=∅h_{0} = \emptyseth0​=∅. Since the policy depends only on the history and not on zzz, its terms cancel in Bayes’ rule, and the posterior is p(z∣ht)∝p(z)∏s=1tp(ys∣z,xs,hs−1).p(z \mid h_{t}) \propto p(z) \prod_{s=1}^{t} p(y_{s} \mid z, x_{s}, h_{s-1}).p(z∣ht​)∝p(z)s=1∏t​p(ys​∣z,xs​,hs−1​). The posterior predictive of the next outcome is p(yt∣xt,ht−1)=∫p(yt∣z,xt,ht−1) p(z∣ht−1) dz.p(y_{t} \mid x_{t}, h_{t-1}) = \int p(y_{t} \mid z, x_{t}, h_{t-1}) \, p(z \mid h_{t-1}) \, \mathrm{d} z.p(yt​∣xt​,ht−1​)=∫p(yt​∣z,xt​,ht−1​)p(z∣ht−1​)dz.

Now, for each zzz, let Et(z)≔p(z∣ht)p(z)(1)E_{t}(z) \coloneqq \frac{p(z \mid h_{t})}{p(z)} \tag{1}Et​(z):=p(z)p(z∣ht​)​(1) be the ratio of posterior to prior, so that E0(z)=1E_{0}(z) = 1E0​(z)=1. This ratio has an interpretation as the wealth process of an oracle who knows the true parameter zzz. To see this, we apply Bayes’ rule repeatedly and factorise the above ratio as Et(z)=∏s=1tp(ys∣z,xs,hs−1)p(ys∣xs,hs−1).(2)E_{t}(z) = \prod_{s=1}^{t} \frac{p(y_{s} \mid z, x_{s}, h_{s-1})}{p(y_{s} \mid x_{s}, h_{s-1})}. \tag{2}Et​(z)=s=1∏t​p(ys​∣xs​,hs−1​)p(ys​∣z,xs​,hs−1​)​.(2) Each factor in the above equation has a betting interpretation. Before ysy_{s}ys​ is revealed, a bookmaker who believes the model but does not know zzz offers fair odds according to the posterior predictive p(⋅∣xs,hs−1)p(\cdot \mid x_{s}, h_{s-1})p(⋅∣xs​,hs−1​). A bettor who knows zzz stakes her whole wealth according to p(⋅∣z,xs,hs−1)p(\cdot \mid z, x_{s}, h_{s-1})p(⋅∣z,xs​,hs−1​), which, by the same argument as Kelly’s theorem applied to a single round, is the growth-optimal bet given her information. Her wealth is then multiplied by the sss-th factor in (2), so Et(z)E_{t}(z)Et​(z) is her wealth after ttt design steps, whichever policy chose the designs.

The Uninformative Null and the EIG

We can now treat one entire experiment as a single round of Kelly’s game. Nature draws z∼p(z)z \sim p(z)z∼p(z), which the oracle receives over the private wire, and the outcome she bets on is the whole history hTh_{T}hT​. The bookmaker, who does not know zzz, prices this outcome at its marginal law p(hT)p(h_{T})p(hT​) under the policy π\piπ; equivalently, by (2), the bookmaker quotes the posterior predictive odds one design step at a time, and the oracle places her bet one step at a time too.

Fix zzz. The natural null hypothesis is that the experiment is uninformative, that is, the data carry no trace of zzz: H0 ⁣:hT∼p(hT)H_{0}\colon h_{T} \sim p(h_{T})H0​:hT​∼p(hT​), against the alternative H1 ⁣:hT∼p(hT∣z)H_{1}\colon h_{T} \sim p(h_{T} \mid z)H1​:hT​∼p(hT​∣z). As before, the policy’s terms cancel in the likelihood ratio, p(hT∣z)p(hT)=p(z∣hT)p(z)=ET(z),(3)\frac{p(h_{T} \mid z)}{p(h_{T})} = \frac{p(z \mid h_{T})}{p(z)} = E_{T}(z), \tag{3}p(hT​)p(hT​∣z)​=p(z)p(z∣hT​)​=ET​(z),(3) so the oracle’s wealth is exactly the likelihood ratio of the alternative against the null, just as MtM_{t}Mt​ was in the testing-by-betting section, and hence the GRO e-variable for this test. It is straightforward to show that, under the null, (Et(z))0≤t≤T(E_{t}(z))_{0 \leq t \leq T}(Et​(z))0≤t≤T​ is a non-negative martingale with E0(z)=1E_{0}(z) = 1E0​(z)=1, so the oracle’s wealth is a test martingale for every zzz. In betting terms, the bookmaker’s odds are fair under the null, so even the oracle cannot expect to make money if zzz leaves no trace in the data. The optimal growth rate of the test is KL⁡[p(hT∣z) ∥ p(hT)]\operatorname{KL}[p(h_{T} \mid z) \,\Vert\, p(h_{T})]KL[p(hT​∣z)∥p(hT​)].

Averaging over the message on the wire, Kelly’s theorem gives the oracle’s growth rate across repeated experiments as Ep(z)[KL⁡[p(hT∣z) ∥ p(hT)]]=I(z;hT)=EIG⁡T(π).(4)\mathbb{E}_{p(z)}\left[\operatorname{KL}[p(h_{T} \mid z) \,\Vert\, p(h_{T})]\right] = I(z; h_{T}) = \operatorname{EIG}_{T}(\pi). \tag{4}Ep(z)​[KL[p(hT​∣z)∥p(hT​)]]=I(z;hT​)=EIGT​(π).(4) That is, the EIG is exactly Kelly’s growth rate for a gambler whose private wire carries zzz, betting on the outcome of the experiment against a bookmaker who believes it is uninformative about zzz.

Conclusion

Seen this way, experimental design is the problem of choosing which game to play. The bookmaker always offers fair odds under the model, so no experiment lets a bettor without knowledge of zzz make money. What the policy π\piπ controls is how much the private wire is worth: an informative experiment is one in which knowing zzz lets the oracle beat the bookmaker quickly, and the EIG-optimal policy is the one that makes this edge as large as possible. In testing terms, maximising the EIG chooses the experiment that, on average over the prior, gathers evidence fastest against the hypothesis that we learn nothing about zzz.

Lindley, D. V. (1956), “On a measure of the information provided by an experiment,” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 27, 986–1005.
Ramdas, A., and Wang, R. (2025), “Hypothesis testing with e-values,” Foundations and Trends in Statistics, 1, 1–390.
Shafer, G. (2021), “Testing by betting: A strategy for statistical and scientific communication,” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A: Statistics in Society, 184, 407–431.
Shafer, G., and Vovk, V. (2019), Game-theoretic foundations for probability and finance, John Wiley & Sons.

entry.title: Measures of Uncertainty are Decision Problems in Disguise
entry.summary:
Measures of Uncertainty are Decision Problems in Disguise

Published on 2026-10-12.

#bayesian-experimental-design

While working on my latest paper on designing experiments for external decision makers, I went down a rabbit hole in the literature on measures of uncertainty. Along the way I came across some interesting old papers that I had either never seen or never bothered to read. Together, they point to one idea: that specifying a reasonable measure of uncertainty is the same thing as specifying a decision problem. This was not obvious to me beforehand, and I suspect it is not obvious to most people who use these measures. This post is my attempt to document this idea for my future self, and for the odd reader with an interest in decision theory or uncertainty quantification.

Decision Theory 101

I will start with a brief review of the setup of Bayesian decision theory (Savage, 1954). Let z∈Zz \in \mathcal{Z}z∈Z denote the hidden state of the world, and let a∈Aa \in \mathcal{A}a∈A denote an action available to us. The state is assumed to carry all information that is relevant for the decision, so that each pair of a state and an action leads to a definite consequence for the decision maker (us). The table below gives an example of a decision problem.

Savage’s classic example of a decision problem about making an omelette, which illustrates acts, states, and consequences (Savage, 1954, Table 1). We start with five good eggs already broken into a bowl, and we need to decide what to do with a sixth egg, which may or may not be rotten.
Action State: Good State: Rotten
break into bowl six-egg omelette no omelette, and five good eggs destroyed
break into saucer six-egg omelette, and a saucer to wash five-egg omelette, and a saucer to wash
throw away five-egg omelette, and one good egg destroyed five-egg omelette

Savage’s theorem says that if our preferences between actions satisfy a handful of axioms, which amount to requiring that we are consistent in what we prefer, then there exist a probability distribution μ\muμ over Z\mathcal{Z}Z and a loss function ℓ:A×Z→R\ell: \mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{Z} \to \mathbb{R}ℓ:A×Z→R such that we prefer one action to another exactly when it has lower expected loss. The distribution μ\muμ represents our beliefs about the hidden state, the loss represents our preferences over consequences, and the rational action is the one that minimises expected loss: a⋆∈arg min⁡a∈AEz∼μ[ℓ(a,z)].a^{\star} \in \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mu}[\ell(a, z)].a⋆∈a∈Aargmin​Ez∼μ​[ℓ(a,z)].

Measures of Uncertainty

Let us now see how a decision problem naturally gives rise to a measure of uncertainty. For a fixed decision problem and a belief μ\muμ over Z\mathcal{Z}Z, consider the quantity Hℓ[μ]≔inf⁡a∈AEz∼μ[ℓ(a,z)]−Ez∼μ[inf⁡a∈Aℓ(a,z)].\mathbb{H}_{\ell}[\mu] \coloneqq \inf_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mu}[\ell(a, z)] - \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mu}\left[\inf_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \ell(a, z)\right].Hℓ​[μ]:=a∈Ainf​Ez∼μ​[ℓ(a,z)]−Ez∼μ​[a∈Ainf​ℓ(a,z)]. The first term is the best expected loss we can achieve without knowing the state, and the second is the expected loss we would achieve if we were told the state before acting. The difference is therefore the expected cost of our uncertainty about zzz. Raiffa and Schlaifer (1961) called it the expected value of perfect information (EVPI): it is the most we should be willing to pay an oracle who will reveal zzz. Note that, once the decision problem is fixed, Hℓ\mathbb{H}_{\ell}Hℓ​ depends on the belief μ\muμ alone; it takes a distribution and returns a number that says how much our ignorance of the state costs us.

If the loss is normalised so that the best action in every state has zero loss, i.e. inf⁡aℓ(a,z)=0\inf_{a} \ell(a, z) = 0infa​ℓ(a,z)=0 for all zzz, the second term vanishes and the EVPI reduces to the Bayes risk, Hℓ[μ]=inf⁡a∈AEz∼μ[ℓ(a,z)].\mathbb{H}_{\ell}[\mu] = \inf_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mu}[\ell(a, z)].Hℓ​[μ]=a∈Ainf​Ez∼μ​[ℓ(a,z)]. This is what Grünwald and Dawid (2004) call a generalised entropy. The Bayes risk makes sense even when the normalisation does not, for instance when inf⁡aℓ(a,z)=−∞\inf_{a} \ell(a, z) = -\inftyinfa​ℓ(a,z)=−∞, and I will use it as the definition of Hℓ\mathbb{H}_{\ell}Hℓ​ from here on.

The property that makes Hℓ\mathbb{H}_{\ell}Hℓ​ interesting is the following. Suppose we hold a belief μ\muμ, observe data YYY, and update to the posterior μY\mu_{Y}μY​. Averaged over the data, the posterior returns the prior: EY[μY]=μ\mathbb{E}_{Y}[\mu_{Y}] = \muEY​[μY​]=μ, where the expectation is under the marginal distribution of YYY implied by μ\muμ and the likelihood. Under mild conditions (all of which hold if ℓ\ellℓ is bounded below, for example),1 we then have EY[Hℓ[μY]]=EY[inf⁡a∈AEz∼μY[ℓ(a,z)]]≤inf⁡a∈AEY[Ez∼μY[ℓ(a,z)]]=inf⁡a∈AEz∼μ[ℓ(a,z)]=Hℓ[μ].\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{Y}\bigl[\mathbb{H}_{\ell}[\mu_{Y}]\bigr] & = \mathbb{E}_{Y}\left[\inf_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mu_{Y}}[\ell(a, z)]\right] \\ & \leq \inf_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{Y} \left[\mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mu_{Y}}[\ell(a, z)]\right] \\ & = \inf_{a \in \mathcal{A}} \mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mu}[\ell(a, z)] = \mathbb{H}_{\ell}[\mu]. \end{aligned}EY​[Hℓ​[μY​]]​=EY​[a∈Ainf​Ez∼μY​​[ℓ(a,z)]]≤a∈Ainf​EY​[Ez∼μY​​[ℓ(a,z)]]=a∈Ainf​Ez∼μ​[ℓ(a,z)]=Hℓ​[μ].​ In words: on average, new information cannot increase H. In terms of the EVPI, the oracle is worth less, on average, once we have seen some data, because part of its job has already been done.

The Equivalence

This property is so natural that it is tempting to turn the argument around and take it as the definition of a measure of uncertainty: a function of the belief that cannot increase on average under any experiment. This is close to what DeGroot (1962) did. Generalising Lindley (1956), who had proved the property for Shannon entropy, DeGroot allowed any non-negative function of the belief to serve as an uncertainty measure, required that no experiment increase it on average, and characterised the functions that satisfy this property. Common measures such as Shannon entropy and variance qualify, and, as we have just seen, so does the generalised entropy of every decision problem.2

The definition is also more than a sanity check, because it pins down the class of measures almost completely. First, it forces concavity. Take any two beliefs μ0\mu_{0}μ0​ and μ1\mu_{1}μ1​, let μ=λμ1+(1−λ)μ0\mu = \lambda \mu_{1} + (1 - \lambda) \mu_{0}μ=λμ1​+(1−λ)μ0​, and consider the experiment that reports Y=1Y = 1Y=1 with probability λ\lambdaλ and Y=0Y = 0Y=0 otherwise, with posteriors μ1\mu_{1}μ1​ and μ0\mu_{0}μ0​. Then the defining property reads H[μ]≥λH[μ1]+(1−λ)H[μ0]\mathbb{H}[\mu] \geq \lambda \mathbb{H}[\mu_{1}] + (1 - \lambda) \mathbb{H}[\mu_{0}]H[μ]≥λH[μ1​]+(1−λ)H[μ0​], which is concavity. Second, on a finite state space the converse holds: a concave function of the belief satisfies the defining property, by Jensen’s inequality applied to the random posterior, since a belief on nnn states is a point in the simplex in Rn\mathbb{R}^{n}Rn (DeGroot, 1962, Theorem 2.1). Third, and this is the step that closes the loop, every non-negative concave function on the simplex is the Bayes risk of some decision problem (Bect and Zhu, 2026; DeGroot, 1962). Put together: on a finite state space, a measure of uncertainty, a concave function of the belief, and the Bayes risk of a decision problem are the same thing.

DeGroot appears to have been the first to draw this conclusion, writing on page 408 that “the distinction sometimes made, as in Lindley (1956), between decision problems and problems in which the experimenter simply wants to gain knowledge may not be very sharp.” He refers to Lindley there because Lindley had proposed the expected information gain (EIG), the expected reduction in Shannon entropy from prior to posterior, precisely as a criterion for the experimenter who has no action in mind and simply wants to “gain knowledge about the state of nature” (Lindley, 1956, p. 987). The explicit decision problem behind the EIG was later written down by Bernardo (1979): take A\mathcal{A}A to be the set of distributions over Z\mathcal{Z}Z and ℓ(a,z)=−log⁡a(z)\ell(a, z) = -\log a(z)ℓ(a,z)=−loga(z), so that the generalised entropy is Shannon entropy and the EIG is the expected reduction in Bayes risk. Bernardo went further and argued that the log loss is the right loss for a pure inference problem, which is the reason the EIG is still the default in Bayesian experimental design.

Caveats and Open Problems

  • The defining property says that H\mathbb{H}H satisfies Jensen’s inequality for random posteriors, and on a finite space this is equivalent to concavity. On infinite spaces concavity remains necessary but is no longer sufficient, and Bect and Zhu (2026, Theorem 5) provide a counterexample.
  • All Bayes risks define valid uncertainty measures, but it is not known whether all valid uncertainty measures can be expressed as Bayes risks for some decision problem. This is Open Problem 2 in Bect and Zhu (2026). On finite spaces the answer is yes (Bect and Zhu, 2026, Theorem 6).

Two Literatures

Something I noticed while researching this post is that the problem of measuring uncertainty and information is studied in both the statistics and economics literature, and the two have almost completely diverged from each other. Both Frankel and Kamenica (2019) and Bect and Zhu (2026) study uncertainty measures, and arrive at essentially the same definition, but the only reference they have in common is the review of proper scoring rules by Gneiting and Raftery (2007). More broadly, the one shared ancestor of the two literatures seems to be Blackwell (1951, 1953). While working on my paper, I would have missed the extremely relevant work of Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011) had Claude not found it while I was searching for related work, and the statistics literature is oblivious to it.

Conclusion

The practical upshot is a question worth asking whenever an uncertainty measure appears in a method: which decision problem is it the Bayes risk of, and is that the problem we actually care about? For entropy the answer is the log loss over predictive distributions, which is a good choice for pure inference and a strange one for almost anything else. The measure is never neutral; it always encodes a loss, whether or not we wrote one down.

Acknowledgements

It was conversations with Tom while we worked on the paper mentioned above that got me started down this path.

References

Bect, J., and Zhu, X. (2026), “Uncertainty functionals revisited: Concavity and Jensen’s inequality,” arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.18100.
Bernardo, J. M. (1979), “Expected information as expected utility,” The Annals of Statistics, 7, 686–690.
Blackwell, D. (1951), “Comparison of experiments,” in Proceedings of the Second Berkeley Symposium on Mathematical Statistics and Probability, University of California Press, pp. 93–103.
Blackwell, D. (1953), “Equivalent comparisons of experiments,” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 24, 265–272.
DeGroot, M. H. (1962), “Uncertainty, information, and sequential experiments,” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 33, 404–419.
Frankel, A., and Kamenica, E. (2019), “Quantifying information and uncertainty,” The American Economic Review, 109, 3650–3680.
Gneiting, T., and Raftery, A. E. (2007), “Strictly proper scoring rules, prediction, and estimation,” Journal of the American Statistical Association, 102, 359–378.
Grünwald, P. D., and Dawid, A. P. (2004), “Game theory, maximum entropy, minimum discrepancy and robust Bayesian decision theory,” The Annals of Statistics, 32, 1367–1433.
Kamenica, E., and Gentzkow, M. (2011), “Bayesian persuasion,” American Economic Review, 101, 2590–2615.
Lindley, D. V. (1956), “On a measure of the information provided by an experiment,” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 27, 986–1005.
Raiffa, H., and Schlaifer, R. (1961), Applied statistical decision theory, Boston: Division of Research, Graduate School of Business Administration, Harvard University.
Savage, L. J. (1954), The foundations of statistics, John Wiley & Sons.

  1. Exchanging the infimum and the expectation requires Hℓ[μY]\mathbb{H}_{\ell}[\mu_{Y}]Hℓ​[μY​] to be quasi-integrable in YYY (Bect and Zhu, 2026). Exchanging the two expectations is the Fubini–Tonelli theorem: it holds whenever ℓ(a,⋅)\ell(a, \cdot)ℓ(a,⋅) is bounded below (Tonelli), or more generally whenever EY[Ez∼μY∣ℓ(a,z)∣]<∞\mathbb{E}_{Y}\bigl[\mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mu_{Y}}|\ell(a, z)|\bigr] < \inftyEY​[Ez∼μY​​∣ℓ(a,z)∣]<∞ for every a∈Aa \in \mathcal{A}a∈A (Fubini).↩︎

  2. Two further conditions are usually added, that the measure is non-negative and that it vanishes on beliefs concentrated on a single state. While these are nice to have, they can both fail for sensible measures on continuous spaces, differential entropy being the standard example.↩︎

entry.title: Asynchronous Data Copies in CuTe DSL
entry.summary:
Asynchronous Data Copies in CuTe DSL

Published on 2026-03-20.

#programming

I’ve always been interested in writing performant code, and recently I’ve been learning how to do that for NVIDIA GPUs. Specifically, I’ve been looking into CuTe DSL, which is a domain-specific language based on Python by NVIDIA. It offers a less verbose and slightly less complicated way to program GPUs compared to writing CUDA C++, but also is more expressive and powerful than Triton.

My ultimate goal is to learn how to write something like FlashAttention 4 in CuTe DSL. However, even a “simple” general matrix multiply (GEMM) kernel for an A100 is about 800 lines of code with many abstractions mixed in, and is difficult for me to grasp, despite the many examples provided on GitHub. The docs are also rather terse. So I thought I’d incrementally work up to complicated kernels, starting from a simple copy kernel to understand how to do asynchronous data copies (which are needed for the fancier kernels).

Prerequisites: I assume a basic familiarity with core GPU programming concepts (see, e.g., sections 1 and 2 of ThunderKittens), as well as some knowledge of CuTe DSL, at the level of the elementwise-addition kernel from the docs. Simon Veitner’s An applied introduction to CuTeDSL and Thread-value layouts in CuTe are great supplements to that example.

Basic info

Our goal in this post is to write a kernel that copies data from a source matrix AAA to a destination matrix BBB, both of shape M×NM \times NM×N. The general idea is to split the source and destination matrices into tiles of a fixed size, and have one thread block (a group of threads that execute on the same streaming multiprocessor) perform the copy for one tile. We will copy source tiles from global memory (GMEM) to shared memory (SMEM) asynchronously, and then copy these to destination tensor blocks on GMEM synchronously. The asynchronous copy is not strictly necessary in this example, but it will be for more complicated kernels where we need to overlap computation with memory operations.

Setup

import torch

import cutlass.cute as cute
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create source and destination matrices
    M, N = 8192, 8192
    src = torch.randn(M, N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
    dst = torch.empty_like(src)

    src_ = from_dlpack(src, assumed_align=16)
    dst_ = from_dlpack(dst, assumed_align=16)

    # Compile and run the kernel
    op = TensorCopyAsync()
    compiled = cute.compile(op, src_, dst_)
    compiled(src_, dst_)

    torch.testing.assert_close(dst, src)

This is straightforward. We create source and destination matrices, both of type float16. The from_dlpack function converts a PyTorch tensor (or a tensor from another DLPack-compatible framework like JAX) into a CuTe tensor with static shape and stride. The TensorCopyAsync class holds the kernel, which we will write next, and after we compile and run it, we verify that dst matches src.

Host code

We initialize the class by providing the number of rows we want in a tile (tile_m) and the number of threads in a thread block (num_threads). We also define a synchronization barrier for the thread block (cta_sync_barrier), where cta stands for “Cooperative Thread Array”, which is CUDA nomenclature for a thread block.

import cutlass
import cutlass.pipeline as pipeline


class TensorCopyAsync:
    def __init__(self, tile_m: int = 32, num_threads: int = 512):
        if num_threads % tile_m != 0:
            raise ValueError("num_threads must be divisible by tile_m")

        self._tile_m = tile_m
        self._num_threads = num_threads
        self.cta_sync_barrier = pipeline.NamedBarrier(
            barrier_id=1, num_threads=num_threads
        )

For the __call__ method, we first calculate the size of the tile based on how many elements we want a single thread to move. Since a single copy instruction can move 32, 64, or 128 bits, here we choose 128, which corresponds to 128 // 16 = 8 elements per thread.

@cute.jit
def __call__(self, mSrc: cute.Tensor, mDst: cute.Tensor):
    copy_bits = 128
    vector_elems = copy_bits // mSrc.element_type.width
    threads_per_row = self._num_threads // self._tile_m
    tile_n = threads_per_row * vector_elems

    if cutlass.const_expr(
        mSrc.shape[0] % self._tile_m != 0 or mSrc.shape[1] % tile_n != 0
    ):
        raise ValueError(
            f"mSrc/mDst shape must be divisible by ({self._tile_m}, {tile_n})"
        )

Here, each thread will copy vector_elems (which is 8) elements which are laid out sequentially in a single row.

The next order of business is to define the copy operations we want. We first want to copy data from src to a staging tile in SMEM, then from that tile back to dst on GMEM. In CuTe, we specify the copy instruction by constructing a CopyAtom, which is a Python class that holds information related to the instruction, such as which copy operation to use and the data type of the elements to be copied. Here we define the two copy atoms: atom_async_copy is for the GMEM to SMEM copy, whereas atom_store is for the reverse.

atom_async_copy = cute.make_copy_atom(
    cute.nvgpu.cpasync.CopyG2SOp(),  # Asynchronous GMEM -> SMEM copy operation
    mSrc.element_type,
    num_bits_per_copy=copy_bits,
)
atom_store = cute.make_copy_atom(
    cute.nvgpu.CopyUniversalOp(),  # General-purpose copy operation
    mDst.element_type,
    num_bits_per_copy=copy_bits,
)

The rest of the code defines a thread-value layout for the tiles, and divides the source and destination tensors according to the layout with cute.zipped_divide. Note the use of cute.make_tiled_copy_tv to create tiled versions of the copy instructions we defined earlier.

thr_layout = cute.make_layout(
    (self._tile_m, threads_per_row), stride=(threads_per_row, 1)
)
val_layout = cute.make_layout((1, vector_elems))
tiled_copy_load = cute.make_tiled_copy_tv(
    atom_async_copy, thr_layout, val_layout
)
tiled_copy_store = cute.make_tiled_copy_tv(atom_store, thr_layout, val_layout)

sSrc_layout = cute.make_layout((self._tile_m, tile_n), stride=(tile_n, 1))
gSrc = cute.zipped_divide(mSrc, (self._tile_m, tile_n))
gDst = cute.zipped_divide(mDst, (self._tile_m, tile_n))

We finally launch the kernel with one tile assigned to one thread block. We use cute.ceil_div to calculate how many tiles we need to cover the entire matrix.

tiles_mn = cute.ceil_div(mSrc.shape, (self._tile_m, tile_n))
self.kernel(
    gSrc,
    gDst,
    sSrc_layout,
    tiled_copy_load,
    tiled_copy_store,
).launch(
    grid=[tiles_mn[1], tiles_mn[0], 1],
    block=[self._num_threads, 1, 1],
)

Device code

For the kernel itself, we start by accessing the source and destination tiles assigned to this thread block.

@cute.kernel
def kernel(
    self,
    gSrc: cute.Tensor,
    gDst: cute.Tensor,
    sSrc_layout: cute.Layout,
    tiled_copy_load: cute.TiledCopy,
    tiled_copy_store: cute.TiledCopy,
):
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    bidx, bidy, _ = cute.arch.block_idx()

    blkSrc = gSrc[((None, None), (bidy, bidx))]
    blkDst = gDst[((None, None), (bidy, bidx))]

This is followed by allocating memory in SMEM, which we will use for staging.

smem = cutlass.utils.SmemAllocator()
sSrc = smem.allocate_tensor(gSrc.element_type, sSrc_layout, 16)

We now need to create copy instructions for the elements of the tile that only the current thread is responsible for. We do this in CuTe using the following snippet (the function names are self-explanatory):

thr_copy_load = tiled_copy_load.get_slice(tidx)
tSgSrc = thr_copy_load.partition_S(blkSrc)
tSsSrc = thr_copy_load.partition_D(sSrc)
cute.copy(tiled_copy_load, tSgSrc, tSsSrc)

When using cute.copy with an asynchronous copy instruction, we also have to use the following code to instruct the GPU to execute it.

cute.arch.cp_async_commit_group()  # Submit this thread's queued operations
cute.arch.cp_async_wait_group(0)  # Wait until this thread's operations are done
self.cta_sync_barrier.arrive_and_wait()  # Sync between all threads in the thread block

We finally copy data from the SMEM tensor to dst.

thr_copy_store = tiled_copy_store.get_slice(tidx)
tSsStore = thr_copy_store.partition_S(sSrc)
tSgDst = thr_copy_store.partition_D(blkDst)
cute.copy(tiled_copy_store, tSsStore, tSgDst)

That’s it! On profiling this kernel with Nsight Compute on an A100, it achieves 87% of the bandwidth of the GPU, which is pretty good.

Parting thoughts

The full code is available here. I tried experimenting with different tile sizes and number of threads, but 87% is the most I could achieve. If you have ideas on how to improve the throughput even more, please send me an email or open a GitHub issue!

Next up is a GEMM kernel for the Ampere generation (following the example here).

entry.title: Steering Language Models with Sequential Monte Carlo
entry.summary:
Steering Language Models with Sequential Monte Carlo

Published on 2025-10-09.

#sequential-monte-carlo #machine-learning

A good chunk of my work as part of my PhD involves using sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods to solve decision-making problems. SMC algorithms are used to efficiently sample from sequences of distributions, and while they are mostly used in physics, signal processing and Bayesian statistics, recently they have also found uses in inference-time alignment of generative models. In this post, I’ll show how I used SMC to “steer” a tiny pre-trained language model into writing sad stories.

Background: How LLMs Generate Text

A language model works over a vocabulary S\mathsf{S}S of tokens. At each step t∈Nt \in \mathbb{N}t∈N, it predicts the probability distribution of the next token given the history so far:

s1:t−1↦p(⋅∣s1:t−1)∈P(S),s_{1:t-1} \mapsto p(\cdot \mid s_{1:t-1}) \in \mathcal{P}(\mathsf{S}),s1:t−1​↦p(⋅∣s1:t−1​)∈P(S),

where P(S)\mathcal{P}(\mathsf{S})P(S) is the set of distributions over the vocabulary S\textsf{S}S and s1:t−1≔{s1,s2,…,st−1}s_{1:t-1} \coloneqq \{ s_{1}, s_{2}, \dots, s_{t-1} \}s1:t−1​:={s1​,s2​,…,st−1​}. Generating text with the language model is the task of sampling a sequence s1:Ts_{1:T}s1:T​ from the joint distribution

PT(s1:T)≔∏t=1Tp(st∣s1:t−1),where s1:0≔∅.\mathbb{P}_{T}(s_{1:T}) \coloneqq \prod_{t=1}^{T} p(s_{t} \mid s_{1:t-1}), \quad \text{where } s_{1:0} \coloneqq \emptyset.PT​(s1:T​):=t=1∏T​p(st​∣s1:t−1​),where s1:0​:=∅.

Inference-Time Alignment of LLMs

Inference-time alignment refers to modifying a pre-trained model’s sampling behavior without changing its parameters. Instead of fine-tuning the model weights, we intervene at sampling time and adjust how likely the model is to pick certain continuations. Sequential Monte Carlo provides a natural framework for this: by iteratively reweighting and resampling partial generations based on a reward signal, we can nudge the model toward desired behaviors while retaining some of its inherent randomness and diversity.

Formally, we specify our preferences through a sequence of reward functions

rt:St→R,t≥1,r_{t}: \mathsf{S}^{t} \to \mathbb{R}, \quad t \geq 1,rt​:St→R,t≥1,

which score partial sequences. This setup is quite general: rtr_trt​ could encode stylistic preferences, safety constraints, or factuality. In my case, rtr_{t}rt​ is just a neural network that has been trained to output a “sadness score” in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] for a given phrase. We then define a new distribution QT\mathbb{Q}_{T}QT​ over sequences, which is tilted towards the cumulative reward:

QT(s1:T)∝PT(s1:T)⋅exp⁡{∑t=1Tη⋅rt(s1:t)},η>0.\mathbb{Q}_{T}(s_{1:T}) \propto \mathbb{P}_{T}(s_{1:T}) \cdot \exp\left\{\sum_{t=1}^{T} \eta \cdot r_{t}(s_{1:t})\right\}, \quad \eta > 0.QT​(s1:T​)∝PT​(s1:T​)⋅exp{t=1∑T​η⋅rt​(s1:t​)},η>0.

Intuitively, QT\mathbb{Q}_TQT​ reweights the model’s likelihoods so that sequences with higher cumulative reward become exponentially more probable.

Sampling from QT\mathbb{Q}_{T}QT​ is straightforward with SMC. The recipe is as follows, with steps 1 and 2 repeated for all n∈{1,…,N},N∈Nn \in \{1, \dots, N\}, N \in \mathbb{N}n∈{1,…,N},N∈N:

  1. Propose: Sample a token stn∼p(⋅∣s1:t−1n)s_{t}^{n} \sim p(\cdot \mid s_{1:t-1}^{n})stn​∼p(⋅∣s1:t−1n​) and append to sequence, s1:tn=(s1:t−1n,stn)s_{1:t}^{n} = (s_{1:t-1}^{n}, s_{t}^{n})s1:tn​=(s1:t−1n​,stn​).
  2. Weight: Compute unnormalized weight wtn=exp⁡{η⋅rt(s1:tn)}w_{t}^{n} = \exp \{ \eta \cdot r_{t}(s_{1:t}^{n}) \}wtn​=exp{η⋅rt​(s1:tn​)}, then normalize: Wtn=wtn/∑m=1NwtmW_{t}^{n} = w_{t}^{n} / \sum_{m=1}^{N} w_{t}^{m}Wtn​=wtn​/∑m=1N​wtm​.
  3. Resample: Draw NNN new particles from {s1:tn}n=1N\{s_{1:t}^n\}_{n=1}^N{s1:tn​}n=1N​ with replacement, proportionally to WtnW_{t}^{n}Wtn​. (This duplicates the ‘sad’ phrases and prunes away overly cheerful ones.)
  4. Repeat: Until t=Tt = Tt=T.

Over time, the population of particles gradually concentrates on high-reward trajectories, in this case the sadder continuations.

Sob Story Time

To illustrate the method, I’m using TinyStories-33M, a language model trained on short children’s stories (Eldan and Li, 2023). Importantly, this model is not fine-tuned for sadness (or anything else), and is just a pure text predictor. The code accompanying this post is available on GitHub.

I gave TinyStories the prompt:

“When the prince came home, he saw”

Here’s what the base model produced (one sample from PT\mathbb{P}_{T}PT​):

“When the prince came home, he saw the heavy bag of jewelry. He wanted to buy it and wear it. He asked the king to sell it to him. The kind king said ‘Yes!’, and …”

Hmm, way too cheerful for our tastes. Now here’s what happens after steering with SMC (one sample from QT\mathbb{Q}_{T}QT​):

“When the prince came home, he saw the sad family sitting by the stove. He felt very sad too. He had lost his rare treasure box and now it was gone forever.”

That’s more like it!

Bonus: Steering as Optimization

A simple but neat result is that the steered distribution QT\mathbb{Q}_{T}QT​ is the minimizer of

L(Q)=EQ[−∑t=1Trt(s1:t)]+1η DKL[Q∥PT],Q∈P(S),\mathcal{L}(Q) = \mathbb{E}_{Q} \left[ -\sum_{t=1}^{T} r_{t}(s_{1:t}) \right] + \frac{1}{\eta} \, \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}} \left[ Q \Vert \mathbb{P}_{T} \right], \quad Q \in \mathcal{P}(\mathsf{S}),L(Q)=EQ​[−t=1∑T​rt​(s1:t​)]+η1​DKL​[Q∥PT​],Q∈P(S),

where DKL\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}DKL​ is the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence (see, e.g., Bissiri et al., 2016). The first term on the RHS is responsible for maximizing the cumulative reward (sadness), while the second term is a regularizer forcing QQQ to stay close to the base model PT\mathbb{P}_{T}PT​. This regularization term prevents collapse into a small number of “super sad” trajectories, thus preserving diversity of model outputs.

This optimization perspective also makes clear the connection to reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF, Ziegler et al., 2020), where the same objective L(Q)\mathcal{L}(Q)L(Q) is minimized by fine-tuning the model weights. Here, we’re skipping the optimization and directly sampling from the minimizer with SMC.

Parting Notes

The algorithm presented here is the simplest version of SMC (known as the “bootstrap” particle filter), and in practice more sophisticated techniques are required to actually deliver on the promise of preserving output diversity. These techniques include adaptive resampling schedules and twisting, see, e.g., Naesseth et al. (2019). For a state-of-the-art application of SMC to language models, I recommend Zhao et al. (2024).

References

Bissiri, P. G., Holmes, C. C., and Walker, S. G. (2016), “A general framework for updating belief distributions,” Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B: Statistical Methodology, 78, 1103–1130.
Eldan, R., and Li, Y. (2023), “TinyStories: How small can language models be and still speak coherent english?”
Naesseth, C. A., Lindsten, F., Schön, T. B., and others (2019), “Elements of sequential Monte Carlo,” Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, 12, 307–392.
Zhao, S., Brekelmans, R., Makhzani, A., and Grosse, R. (2024), “Probabilistic inference in language models via twisted sequential Monte Carlo,” in International Conference on Machine Learning.
Ziegler, D. M., Stiennon, N., Wu, J., Brown, T. B., Radford, A., Amodei, D., Christiano, P., and Irving, G. (2020), “Fine-tuning language models from human preferences.”

entry.title: Using LaTeX Snippets in Markdown Files in Neovim
entry.summary:
Using LaTeX Snippets in Markdown Files in Neovim

Published on 2025-09-24.

#neovim #latex

I frequently write notes in Markdown using Neovim, and many of those notes contain math. Unfortunately, all of my handy LaTeX snippets created with LuaSnip don’t work in Markdown, which makes it a pain to write anything beyond the simplest equations. In this post, I document how I got my snippets working in Markdown.

Basic Setup

The first step is to tell LuaSnip to load LaTeX snippets in Markdown files. This saves us from having to duplicate all our LaTeX snippets. Since I use lazy.nvim as my package manager, I just had to tweak the config function like this:

config = function()
  local ls = require("luasnip")

  ls.config.set_config({
    ...
  })

  -- Make TeX snippets available in markdown
  ls.filetype_extend("markdown", { "tex" })

  ...
end,

It turns out that this is all we need to get basic snippet functionality working. However, many of my snippets use conditional expansion, with snippets only expanding if the cursor is inside a math environment. For example, typing ff automatically expands to \frac{}{} when I’m inside dollar signs or an align environment, but it won’t expand when I type ‘affirm’ or ‘puff’ in normal text. Since a lot of my go-to snippets rely on this, that’s the next thing I set up.

Conditional Expansion in Math Environments

When I write LaTeX files, I rely on a package called VimTex for syntax highlighting and a bunch of other useful features. One of its perks is that it can detect math environments, which we can use as a condition for snippet expansion with the following Lua function (see the article by ejmastnak for more details):

tex_utils.in_math = function()
  -- This function requires the VimTeX plugin.
  return vim.fn["vimtex#syntax#in_mathzone"]() == 1
end

But VimTeX is a filetype-specific plugin, so it only loads for .tex files. To get the same functionality in Markdown, we need to create a nvim/after/syntax/markdown.vim file with the following contents:

" From https://github.com/lervag/vimtex/issues/2395
if exists('b:current_syntax')
  unlet b:current_syntax
endif

syn include @tex syntax/tex.vim
syn region markdownMath start="\\\@<!\$" end="\$" skip="\\\$" contains=@tex keepend
syn region markdownMath start="\\\@<!\$\$" end="\$\$" skip="\\\$" contains=@tex keepend

let b:current_syntax = 'markdown'

This snippet first clears any existing Markdown syntax settings, then tells Neovim to pull in LaTeX syntax rules from syntax/tex.vim (provided by VimTeX). It defines $...$ and $$...$$ as math environments, so anything inside them gets highlighted and treated like LaTeX math, even in a Markdown file.

Bonus for VimWiki Users

If you use VimWiki for note-taking and also rely on the <Tab> key for snippet expansion, you’ll need to free up <Tab> in insert mode, since VimWiki already uses it for shortcuts. I solved this by adding the following autocommand for VimWiki:

config = function()
  vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd("FileType", {
    pattern = "vimwiki",
    callback = function()
      -- Disable <Tab> in insert mode.
      vim.keymap.del("i", "<Tab>", { buffer = true })
    end,
  })
end,

Conclusion

That’s it, we’re all set! We’re now ready to give Giles Castel a run for his money in Markdown ;). That said, this setup is not perfect. The biggest limitation is that it only recognizes math environments defined with single or double dollar signs, so conditional snippets won’t work inside environments like align. This is not a huge deal for me though, since all serious math gets done in .tex files. If you’re curious, you can check out my full Neovim configuration here.

entry.title: Expected Information as Expected Utility
entry.summary:
Expected Information as Expected Utility

Published on 2025-06-08.

#bayesian-experimental-design

Imagine a scientist planning a clinical trial to determine the optimal dosage of a new diabetes drug. Due to constraints on budget and patient safety, only a limited number of tests can be conducted, so the scientist must decide which dosage levels to test to most effectively learn the relationship between dose and patient response. To make these decisions systematically, the scientist can turn to Bayesian experimental design (BED), which is a principled framework for designing optimal experiments under uncertainty.

Suppose the scientist models the dose–response relationship using a parametric form governed by unknown parameters θ∈Θ\theta \in \Thetaθ∈Θ—such as the maximum effect of the drug, the dose achieving half that effect, and the baseline response. To learn about these parameters, she must choose a design ξ\xiξ, which could specify, for example, a set of dosage levels and how patients are allocated to them. A widely used objective in BED is to choose the design that maximizes the expected information gain (EIG) (Lindley, 1956):

EIG(ξ)≔Ep(y∣ξ)[H[pθ(θ)]−H[pθ∣y,ξ(θ)]].\mathrm{EIG}(\xi) \coloneqq \mathbb{E}_{p(y \mid \xi)} \Bigl[ \mathbb{H} \bigl[ p_{\theta}(\theta) \bigr] - \mathbb{H} \bigl[ p_{\theta \mid y, \xi}(\theta) \bigr] \Bigr].EIG(ξ):=Ep(y∣ξ)​[H[pθ​(θ)]−H[pθ∣y,ξ​(θ)]].

It quantifies how much we expect to reduce our uncertainty about θ\thetaθ, starting from some prior belief pθp_{\theta}pθ​, on applying the design ξ\xiξ. Here, H\mathbb{H}H denotes Shannon entropy (or differential entropy for continuous θ\thetaθ), and the expectation is over possible outcomes yyy with distribution p(y∣ξ)p(y \mid \xi)p(y∣ξ).

The EIG is intuitive—it is the expected reduction in entropy from prior to posterior. But intuition aside, it raises a natural question. The reduction in Shannon entropy is only one of many ways to measure uncertainty reduction, or even more generally, the utility of an experiment (ξ,y)(\xi, y)(ξ,y) (Huan et al., 2024). Is there, then, any fundamental reason to prefer the EIG over alternative utility measures?

It turns out the answer is yes. In Bernardo (1979), José M. Bernardo, a student of Dennis Lindley, gave a justification for the EIG grounded in decision theory. He showed that the EIG arises naturally from a decision problem under reasonable assumptions on the utility function. I find this result extremely remarkable, and this is an appreciation post about a half-century later :)

The Decision-Theoretic Setup

Consider a decision problem where a scientist has to report a distribution q∈P(Θ)q \in \mathcal{P}(\Theta)q∈P(Θ) for θ\thetaθ, where the decision space P(Θ)\mathcal{P}(\Theta)P(Θ) is the set of probability measures on Θ\ThetaΘ.1 The utility obtained if she reports qqq when the true parameter is θ\thetaθ is quantified by means of a utility function u:P(Θ)×Θ→Ru:\mathcal{P}(\Theta) \times \Theta \to \mathbb{R}u:P(Θ)×Θ→R.2 Suppose the scientist applies a design ξ\xiξ and observes an outcome yyy, after which she updates her belief to pθ∣y,ξ(θ)p_{\theta \mid y, \xi}(\theta)pθ∣y,ξ​(θ) using Bayes’ rule. Then, her expected utility when reporting qqq is

∫u(q,θ) pθ∣y,ξ(dθ).\int u(q, \theta) \, p_{\theta \mid y, \xi}(d\theta).∫u(q,θ)pθ∣y,ξ​(dθ).

The second restriction we need on the utility function is that it is local, i.e., u(q,θ)=u(q(θ),θ)u(q, \theta) = u\bigl(q(\theta), \theta\bigr)u(q,θ)=u(q(θ),θ) for all θ∈Θ\theta \in \Thetaθ∈Θ. The striking result of Bernardo (1979) is that if the utility function uuu is strictly proper, local, and sufficiently smooth (as a function of qqq), then it is of the form

Now, the gain in expected utility for the scientist from the experiment (ξ,y)(\xi, y)(ξ,y) is

which simplifies to

A⋅Ey∣ξ[H[pθ(θ)]−H[pθ∣y,ξ(θ)]]+Ey∣ξ[Eθ∣y,ξ[B(θ)]−Eθ[B(θ)]]⏟=0=A⋅EIG(ξ).\begin{align*} & A \cdot \mathbb{E}_{y \mid \xi}\Bigl[ \mathbb{H}\bigl[p_{\theta}(\theta)\bigr] - \mathbb{H}\bigl[ p_{\theta \mid y, \xi}(\theta) \bigr] \Bigr] + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{y \mid \xi} \Bigl[ \mathbb{E}_{\theta \mid y, \xi}[B(\theta)] - \mathbb{E}_{\theta}[B(\theta)] \Bigr]}_{=0} \\ & = A \cdot \mathrm{EIG}(\xi). \end{align*}​A⋅Ey∣ξ​[H[pθ​(θ)]−H[pθ∣y,ξ​(θ)]]+=0Ey∣ξ​[Eθ∣y,ξ​[B(θ)]−Eθ​[B(θ)]]​​=A⋅EIG(ξ).​

This shows that, for the purpose of choosing the best design, the choice of AAA and BBB is irrelevant, and the utility function can simply be the log density, u(q,θ)=log⁡q(θ)u(q, \theta) = \log q(\theta)u(q,θ)=logq(θ).

Concluding Remarks

To motivate his paper, Bernardo writes in the abstract:

… a scientist typically does not have, nor can be normally expected to have, a clear idea of the utility of his results.

By considering a decision problem of choosing the best distribution to report, and showing that the EIG arises naturally under reasonable assumptions on the utility function, Bernardo makes a compelling argument for using the EIG in precisely those settings where the scientist cannot quantify the utility of her results a priori.
